content: The document outlines the World Health Organization's (WHO) guidelines for testing the efficacy of spatial repellents, which are products designed to reduce human contact with disease-carrying insects, particularly mosquitoes, by altering their behavior through airborne chemicals. These repellents aim to provide personal protection by reducing mosquito attraction, feeding, or movement toward humans. The guidelines are intended to standardize testing procedures and promote the development of novel active ingredients with spatial repellent properties for public health purposes. The guidelines detail laboratory, semi-field, and field testing methods for evaluating the efficacy of spatial repellents. Laboratory studies focus on determining the inherent properties of active ingredients (AIs) under controlled conditions, including their ability to repel mosquitoes, inhibit host attraction, and prevent feeding. These studies also establish dose-response relationships and effective dosages (ED50 and ED95) for spatial repellency and host attraction inhibition. Field trials assess the protective efficacy of formulated products in real-world settings, measuring the reduction in mosquito landings, feeding, or entry into treated spaces. The duration of protection and optimal dosages are evaluated under standardized conditions. Products are tested in free-flight rooms or other controlled environments, with comparisons made to standard or positive control products. The guidelines emphasize the importance of safety assessments, including toxicity evaluations, before testing. All testing must adhere to ethical regulations, and personnel involved in the studies must receive adequate training. Data reporting should be detailed enough to allow comparisons across multiple evaluation sites. These methods involve introducing mosquitoes into test systems, exposing them to chemical stimuli, and recording their movement, attraction, or inhibition. The spatial activity index (SAI) is calculated to quantify repellency, with values ranging from -1 (indicating attraction) to 1 (indicating repellency). The guidelines also address the evaluation of spatial repellents against insecticide-resistant mosquito strains to assess their effectiveness in disease control strategies. Additionally, they provide recommendations for testing the efficacy of products in reducing vector entry and resting in treated spaces. Overall, the document provides a comprehensive framework for evaluating spatial repellents, ensuring their safety, efficacy, and potential public health value in controlling vector-borne diseases.
